title: Designing a stock exchange

facts.text: A modern exchange achieves microsecond latency by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage.
An order is first followed through the trading flow, which is the critical path with strict latency requirements, so everything in it has to happen fast.
The market data flow and the reporting flow are not on the critical path, and they have different latency requirements from the trading flow.
The critical path starts when an order comes into the order manager, passes mandatory risk checks, is matched, and ends when the execution comes back out of the order manager.
Other, non-critical tasks should be removed from the critical path.
All the components are deployed on a single giant server, with no containers.
Shared memory serves as the event bus between the components, and no hard disk is used.
The order manager and the matching engine are single-threaded on the critical path and each is pinned to a CPU, so there is no context switch and no locks.
The single-threaded application loop executes tasks one by one in sequence.
Other components listen on the event bus and react accordingly.

notes: thin: the two guides give only the critical path and the single-server, shared-memory, single-threaded design; no requirements, order types, order book, matching rules, data model, API, volumes or failover; the 14 steps of the trading flow are in a diagram the text does not spell out.

title: Low-latency critical path design

definition.text: Getting very low latency by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage.

facts.text: A modern stock exchange reaches microsecond latency with the principle of doing less on the critical path.

Tasks that are not critical should be removed from the critical path; for example the market data flow and the reporting flow are off the exchange's critical path and have different latency requirements.
Key components on the critical path can be single-threaded, each pinned to a CPU, so there is no context switch and no locks, and run one task after another in a single loop.
Components can talk through shared memory used as an event bus instead of a hard disk, and be deployed together on one giant server without containers.

notes: General principle drawn from the exchange guides; the exchange itself is in the Worked example.
